name: Chêne de Nerthe

location.address: In the pine forest near the hamlet of Nerthe, on an old airial (forest clearing with house ruins), commune of Magescq

access: Free, on foot. The tree stands on privately owned pine-plantation land within an old airial but is openly and regularly visited by hikers, joggers and mountain bikers via a forestry track from the Nerthe hamlet (about 1km walk each way, difficult by car); no gate, fence or restriction signage was found in any source. The Magescq tourist office also runs a separate, optional guided minibus tour in summer (booking required for that specific tour only, not for general access).
transport: No public transport reaches the site. Nearest town with an SNCF station is Dax (TGV), roughly 10km away; from there it is a drive to the forestry track near Nerthe hamlet, then a ~1km walk on foot.
story:
In August 2010 this oak shed a single branch that measured 3.3 metres around. A month later, on 18 September, the A.R.B.R.E.S. association hung an Arbre Remarquable de France label on what was left: 6.50 metres of trunk at chest height, under a crown 27 metres up.

It grew up alone. The oak stands on an airial, one of the clearings where Landes farmers built their houses among the pines, and the farm here is ruins. The nearest occupied house is two or three kilometres off down a forestry track. For most of its life its only visitors were whoever happened along that track, joggers and hikers and mountain bikers, and nobody wrote any of it down until the label arrived.

Its age is an argument nobody has settled. Local tradition says 600 years, the official label rounds that up to 600 or 700, and growth-rate calculations worked from the girth come out lower, at 500 to 600. Nobody has cored it, so the honest answer is somewhere in the 500 to 700 range.

After the branch came down, visitors reported the wound being dressed with tar, and they kept coming. Four separate hiking platforms now publish routes out to it, the newest of them from 2023. The last kilometre is on foot, which is a good part of why it stayed unknown for so long.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 6.50 metres round at chest height under a crown 27 metres up. It stands alone on the old airial, a clearing in the pine forest, with the ruins of the farm buildings around it.

name: If commun de Nicorps

location.address: Churchyard of the Eglise Saint-Corneille, Nicorps

access: Free. It stands in the churchyard/cemetery of the Eglise Saint-Corneille, a village church with a public cemetery, open in daylight hours; no restriction found in any source.
transport: No specific transit stop found. Nicorps is a small village about 6km south-west of Coutances (which has an SNCF station); reaching the village itself requires a car or bicycle from Coutances.
story:
In October 1987 a hurricane took roughly seven metres off the top of this yew. It has grown most of them back.

The record is unusually good, because people keep measuring it. On 11 June 1930 the naturalist Henri Gadeau de Kerville taped the trunk at 6.28 metres and the crown at 18.50 for his survey of Normandy's old trees. When the CAUE de la Manche came back on 10 November 1998, the storm had cost the tree a major limb and the crown stood under 12 metres, while the trunk had thickened to 7.15. Aerial photographs from 1947 onwards show the canopy retreating on the north-east side. The crown is back to around 16 metres now, and the 1998 dossier describes the girth as still increasing, which makes 7.15 a floor rather than a figure.

Its age comes from the church's own account, which puts it at 600 years. A photographer once captioned a picture of it "l'if millénaire", and that thousand-year claim circulates with nothing behind it, so the six centuries are the number to work from and the millennium is village talk. Call it somewhere between 500 and 700.

This is a churchyard tree in a village of a few hundred people, and that is the honest scale of it. Buried in the same ground: a missionary, a professor of medicine, and Émile Daireaux, who founded a town in Argentina that still carries his name.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by size: two yews stand in the churchyard of Saint-Corneille and this is the larger, over seven metres round, with a crown that stops short at about 16 metres where the 1987 storm took its top.

name: If de Jauzé

location.address: Le bourg, next to the church, 72110 Jauzé

access: Free (confirmed explicitly by the regional tourism board's own listing: 'Acces au site gratuit: Oui'). It stands in the village ('le bourg'), by the church, not on enclosed private land.
transport: No public transport found serving Jauzé, a small village in Sarthe; reachable by car. Nearest larger town is La Ferte-Bernard (SEPENES, the association that inventories Sarthe's remarkable trees, is based there), a short drive away.
story:
The oldest tree in the Sarthe stands beside the church in Jauzé, a village most of France has never heard of. SEPENES, the association that keeps the department's inventory of remarkable trees, calls it le doyen de la Sarthe and puts it at seven to nine centuries, on a trunk 5.70 metres round.

Local tradition goes further and has Vikings planting it, eight hundred to a thousand years ago. The regional tourism board repeats that story and calls it a legend in the same breath, which is the right way round. A visitor's photo caption elsewhere calls it the thousand-year yew. Nobody has produced a source for either figure, so the seven to nine centuries stands: it is the number the people who measured the tree are willing to put their name to.

It carries one genuinely unusual credential. It is the only classified yew in the Sarthe that flowers as a male. Yews come in separate sexes, and the females, the ones that carry red arils in autumn, are what churchyards usually keep; this one sheds pollen in late winter instead.

Access is free and it stands in the open in the bourg, not behind a wall. Reaching Jauzé takes a car. It is a regional tree rather than a national one, but if you are working your way through the old yews of France, this is the one the Sarthe puts forward.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 5.70 metres round, standing in the open in the village centre beside the church rather than inside an enclosure. It is the only tree of that bulk in the bourg.

best_time.label: late winter, when the male flowers open and shed pollen

name: Le Sully de Pesselières

location.address: Pesselières, a hamlet of the commune of Sougères-en-Puisaye

access: Free. It stands in the open hamlet of Pesselières (references place it near the 'rue du chateau' and 'place des halles', both public streets/square), not on enclosed private land.
transport: No public transport found. Pesselières is a small hamlet within Sougères-en-Puisaye, Yonne (Burgundy); reachable by car or as part of a countryside walk (Visorando lists 13 different hiking routes passing it).
story:
France has hundreds of trees called a Tilleul de Sully. This one has a birth year, and a party to prove it.

Maximilien de Béthune, Duke of Sully and Henri IV's chief roads officer, spent the years after the Wars of Religion pressing villages to plant a lime or an elm by the church or on the square. Most of the trees carrying his name inherited it by association. Le Sully de Pesselières is dated: planted in 1598, according to the regional paper L'Yonne républicaine, which is also why the hamlet held two days of festivities for its four hundredth birthday in 1998. That puts it at about 428 years now.

Pesselières is a hamlet inside the commune of Sougères-en-Puisaye, and the lime stands out in the open near the rue du château and the old halles. There is a photograph of it from the early twentieth century and more from 2008 and 2014, so the last hundred years of it are on record, which is rare for a tree this far off the main roads.

Nobody has published a measurement of the trunk. Surveys of other Sully limes put the type at five to seven metres round, but those are other trees. If you go with a tape measure, tell us the number and we will add it.

Thirteen walking routes through the Puisaye pass it, which is roughly what Sully had in mind: a tree where the road goes.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by where it stands, out in the open in the hamlet between the rue du château and the old halles rather than in a garden or a churchyard. It is the lime that carries the Sully name here.
